articleMarkdown:
# Learning from Keeping Still (Gèn): stop at the right time and in the right way

Know when to stop and gather your attention, and also when it is time to act again.

Gen takes the mountain as its image. Its six lines move from toes and calves through waist and back to the body, cheeks, and a substantial kind of stillness. It does not merely teach immobility. It repeatedly asks where stopping happens, whether it is appropriate, and whether excessive force creates new tension. Reading Gen is also learning the boundaries of action.

艮 is hexagram 52 in the traditional King Wen sequence, with the symbol ䷳. Its lower trigram is 艮☶ and its upper trigram is 艮☶, traditionally associated with mountain and mountain respectively. Count the lines from the bottom: 初六, 六二, 九三, 六四, 六五, 上九. A solid line is yang; a broken line is yin. Nine and six identify yang and yin in the line labels; they do not add extra lines.

Line structure (bottom to top): 0 0 1 0 0 1

Six-line figure, displayed top to bottom; line numbering starts at the bottom.

```text
━━━━━━━━━  上九
━━━━ ━━━━  六五
━━━━ ━━━━  六四
━━━━━━━━━  九三
━━━━ ━━━━  六二
━━━━ ━━━━  初六
```

## The judgment

艮：艮其背，不獲其身，行其庭，不見其人，无咎。

Original editorial rendering, not a quotation from Legge: Stillness: stilling the back, not apprehending one’s body. Walking in the courtyard, one does not see its people. No blame.

The judgment connects back, body, courtyard, and people in highly compressed language. Legge understands it through stopping in one’s proper place, while acknowledging that some expressions are difficult to explain. This article does not interpret “not apprehending one’s body” as a requirement to lose awareness of oneself, nor as a description of psychological or neurological symptoms.

For modern study, consider returning attention to what you are responsible for instead of being pulled by every outside stimulus. Stopping does not mean refusing communication, ignoring others, or escaping responsibility. Whether to stop depends on the particular object and situation.

Sources: [zhouyi-52](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=周易/艮&oldid=10647135), [legge1882-52](https://tianmu.org/good-work-library/confucian/general-texts/the-i-ching-james-legge)

## Interpretation in the Ten Wings

The Commentary on the Judgment and the Commentary on the Images belong to the Yi Zhuan, the commentaries usually called the “Ten Wings.” Here their explanations are kept distinct from the judgment and line texts, before turning to modern applications for study.

The Commentary on the Judgment explicitly says to stop when it is time to stop and to move when it is time to move, so that neither movement nor stillness misses its moment. This is an important limit in understanding Gen: stillness is not always superior to action.

The Commentary on the Images depicts two mountains and speaks of thought not going beyond one’s position. This article draws on recognizing responsibility and the scope of attention. It does not turn the phrase into a prohibition on curiosity or questions, or a command to accept an established hierarchy forever.

Sources: [zhouyi-52](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=周易/艮&oldid=10647135), [hon-sep](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/chinese-change/)

## 初六 · A pause can come before an action begins

艮其趾，无咎，利永貞。

Original editorial rendering, not a quotation from Legge: Stilling the toes. No blame; lasting constancy is beneficial.

Toes stand at the beginning of walking. Legge understands stilling them as appropriate self-restraint before an undertaking has started.

Before answering an upsetting message, check whether you have understood it correctly. The brief pause is meant to support a better response, not to delay dealing with it forever.

Sources: [zhouyi-52](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=周易/艮&oldid=10647135), [legge1882-52](https://tianmu.org/good-work-library/confucian/general-texts/the-i-ching-james-legge)

## 六二 · Your pause may not change the whole chain of dependence

艮其腓，不拯其隨，其心不快。

Original editorial rendering, not a quotation from Legge: Stilling the calves; unable to rescue what one follows. The heart is unhappy.

腓 refers to the calf. The ancient text also describes being unable to rescue what one follows, with resulting unhappiness. Legge explains constrained action through the dependent relationship between parts of the body.

In cooperation, recognizing the need to pause may not immediately let you change the overall arrangement. Present your reasons clearly, state your own boundaries, and seek coordination rather than counting every result as your personal responsibility.

Sources: [zhouyi-52](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=周易/艮&oldid=10647135), [legge1882-52](https://tianmu.org/good-work-library/confucian/general-texts/the-i-ching-james-legge)

## 九三 · Rigidly forcing a stop can also cause harm

艮其限，裂其夤，厲薰心。

Original editorial rendering, not a quotation from Legge: Stilling the waist, splitting the muscles along the spine. Danger troubles the heart.

限 and 夤 concern the waist and back. Tearing and a heart troubled as though by scorching make the image tense. Legge reads unease caused by excessive repression. The line is not an instruction for a healthy meditation posture.

If “concentration” becomes a continual effort to force every feeling away, reconsider the method. Appropriate rest, adjustments to tasks, and support are worth considering before stronger control intended to prove self-discipline.

Sources: [zhouyi-52](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=周易/艮&oldid=10647135), [legge1882-52](https://tianmu.org/good-work-library/confucian/general-texts/the-i-ching-james-legge)

## 六四 · Bring the actions you can answer for under control

艮其身，无咎。

Original editorial rendering, not a quotation from Legge: Stilling the body; no blame.

This line directly describes stilling the body. Legge emphasizes controlling one’s own actions without claiming complete control of every inner activity.

During an argument, first restrain expressions that could hurt someone and explain if you need to talk later. You can take responsibility for your conduct without requiring the other person to feel the same emotions immediately.

Sources: [zhouyi-52](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=周易/艮&oldid=10647135), [legge1882-52](https://tianmu.org/good-work-library/confucian/general-texts/the-i-ching-james-legge)

## 六五 · Give speech order and proportion

艮其輔，言有序，悔亡。

Original editorial rendering, not a quotation from Legge: Stilling the jaws; speech has order. Regret disappears.

輔 concerns the cheeks and mouth. Ordered speech connects stopping with expression. Legge follows the reading about words having order; the emphasis is not on total silence.

In an important explanation, give the facts first, then their effects, then the question you need to raise. Removing impulsive judgments often makes the words that genuinely matter easier to hear.

Sources: [zhouyi-52](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=周易/艮&oldid=10647135), [legge1882-52](https://tianmu.org/good-work-library/confucian/general-texts/the-i-ching-james-legge)

## 上九 · Mature stillness need not be rigid or ostentatious

敦艮，吉。

Original editorial rendering, not a quotation from Legge: Substantial, wholehearted stillness. Favorable.

Legge explains 敦艮 as substantial, settled stillness in an appropriate place. It differs from the tense, forced stopping of the third line.

Being able to close the day’s agreed work calmly, without continually looking for more tasks to prove yourself, is also an ability. Such stopping has a clear basis and leaves room to act again tomorrow.

Sources: [zhouyi-52](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=周易/艮&oldid=10647135), [legge1882-52](https://tianmu.org/good-work-library/confucian/general-texts/the-i-ching-james-legge)

## Pausing a discussion when opinions clash

Original modern scenario

Two collaborators become increasingly agitated in a discussion. One notices that he has begun repeating accusations. Rather than disappearing abruptly, he explains that the discussion is no longer productive and proposes returning to it later with specific questions.

During the pause, he organizes what they already agree on, the facts still in dispute, and the parts he can take responsibility for. When they speak again, he checks the facts before explaining the adjustments needed.

The pause serves later action and respects the other person’s need to know what is happening. Gen’s modern application is not about who stays most silent, but whether a pause reduces unhelpful reactions and allows the matter to be handled appropriately.

## Avoiding misreadings

- Gen does not require freezing the body, suppressing feelings, or ignoring real needs. Its bodily imagery is not guidance for medicine, psychotherapy, or exercise.

- “Thought not going beyond one’s position” should not justify banning questions, limiting someone’s development, or refusing necessary responsibility.

## Three exercises

1. Choose something you often struggle to stop doing and define when the responsibility for this occasion is complete.

2. Write a clear explanation for a conversation that needs a pause, including when or under what conditions it will resume.

3. Check whether this pause restores judgment or avoids a question that still needs an answer.

## Related reading

Zhen — Thunder (hexagram-51): Zhen presents responses to a sudden disturbance; Gen emphasizes appropriate stopping. Reading them together can teach adjustment between motion and stillness as circumstances change, rather than dividing people into types that should naturally be impulsive or always quiet.

When reading Gen, ask: has my pause made the next step clearer, or merely pushed away what needs to be faced?

## Textual note

The third line uses the variant 薰 explicitly listed by the base text, whose main reading is 閽. The fifth uses the variant 序, where the main text reads 孚.
